cues.text: Chapter five: Indexing.
Let us begin with the central idea.
An index is an auxiliary structure that maps search keys to records or to other pages.
Think of the index at the back of a textbook: instead of reading every page to find a topic, you look the topic up, and it tells you where to go.
A database index does the same job.
It is extra to the table itself, and its purpose is to help the database find data quickly.
Now, some classical terminology.
A primary index is associated with an ordered primary-key organisation.
A secondary index, by contrast, supports other access paths, meaning other ways of reaching the data besides the primary key.
Next, two ways of describing how much an index stores.
A dense index has an entry for every search-key record or value.
A sparse index omits some entries and relies on the ordering of the data to fill the gap.
So with a sparse index, you find the nearest entry and then follow the order from there.
Then there is the question of physical placement.
Clustered indexes organise the data, or approximate physical locality, so that records with similar keys sit near one another.
Nonclustered indexes reference records that are stored separately.
One caution from the source: terminology differs across database management systems, so always check what a particular product means by these words.
Now to the most common index structures.
B-tree and B-plus-tree indexes keep keys ordered in a balanced hierarchy.
B-plus trees commonly store record references in their leaf pages, and the leaves are connected to one another, which makes range scans efficient.
A range scan means reading all keys between two values, for example every visit between two dates.
Searching follows a path: from the root, through the internal nodes, down to a leaf.
The cost is roughly logarithmic in the number of keys, under ordinary assumptions.
That means that even when the number of keys grows enormously, the number of steps grows only slowly.
If a search returns k matching records, there is additional work to output those k results, on top of the search itself.
Hash indexes work differently.
They map equality keys to buckets, and they must include collision handling, for when different keys land in the same bucket.
Because a hash scatters keys rather than keeping them in order, hash indexes are not suited to ordered range access.
They are for equality lookups.
Now let us look at an example in SQL.
The first statement creates an index named idx underscore visit underscore patient underscore time.
It is created on the visit table, and it covers two columns: patient underscore id, followed by visited underscore at in descending order.
The second statement is a query.
It selects all columns from visit where patient underscore id equals forty-two, orders the results by visited underscore at descending, and limits the output to twenty rows.
The point of the example is the match between the index and the query.
The index groups entries by patient, and within each patient keeps them ordered by visit time, newest first.
So the query can find patient forty-two's entries and read the latest twenty in order, without having to sort.
The source presents this as an illustration of the design, not as an executed result.
Now, more kinds of index.
A composite index is ordered by its column sequence.
The leading key, the first column, often matters for efficient filtering and sorting.
In our example, patient id comes first, which is why filtering by patient is efficient.
A covering index contains all the attributes a query needs.
Whether that actually enables index-only execution, where the table itself need not be read, depends on engine specifics.
Unique indexes enforce uniqueness, so that no two entries share the same key.
Partial indexes cover only selected rows.
Expression indexes cover computed expressions rather than raw columns.
And bitmap indexes are useful for some analytical workloads with low cardinality, meaning columns with few distinct values.
The source adds a distinction: bitmap scans are not the same thing as stored bitmap indexes.
One is an execution technique; the other is a structure kept on disk.
Finally, the costs and the discipline.
Indexes cost storage, and they cost write maintenance, because every insert, update or delete must also keep the indexes up to date.
So select indexes from actual query patterns, and inspect query plans to see what the database really does.
Remove redundant indexes only after checking dependencies, since something may rely on them.
One practical pitfall: a predicate such as LOWER of name may not exploit a normal index on name efficiently, because the index holds the original values, not the lowercased ones.
An expression index, or an appropriate collation, may help.
And the closing advice is simple: avoid blindly indexing every column.
